{{Short description|Type of infinite structure}}
In [[mathematical logic]], and more specifically in [[model theory]], an infinite [[structure (mathematical logic)|structure]] <math>(M,<,\dots)</math> that is [[Total order|totally ordered]] by <math> < </math> is called an '''o-minimal structure''' if and only if every [[definable set|definable]] subset <math>X\subseteq M</math> (with parameters taken from <math>M</math>) is a finite [[union (set theory)|union]] of [[interval (mathematics)|interval]]s and points.

O-minimality can be regarded as a weak form of [[quantifier elimination]]. A structure <math>M</math> is o-minimal if and only if every [[formula (logic)|formula]] with one [[free variable]] and parameters in <math>M</math> is equivalent to a quantifier-free formula involving only the ordering, also with parameters in <math>M</math>. This is analogous to the [[strongly minimal theory|minimal]] structures, which are exactly the analogous property down to equality.

A [[Theory (mathematical logic)|theory]] <math>T</math> is an '''o-minimal theory''' if every [[Model (model theory)|model]] of <math>T</math> is o-minimal. It is known that the [[complete theory]] <math>T</math> of an o-minimal structure is an o-minimal theory.<ref>Knight, Pillay and Steinhorn (1986), Pillay and Steinhorn (1988).</ref> This result is remarkable because, in contrast, the complete theory of a minimal structure need not be a [[strongly minimal theory]], that is, there may be an [[elementarily equivalent]] structure that is not minimal.

==Set-theoretic definition==

O-minimal structures can be defined without recourse to model theory.  Here we define a structure on a nonempty set <math>M</math> in a set-theoretic manner, as a sequence <math>(S_n)_{n=0}^\infty</math> such that
# <math>S_n</math> is a [[Boolean algebra (structure)|boolean algebra]] of subsets of <math>M^n</math>
# if <math>D\in S_n</math> then <math>M\times D</math> and <math>D\times M</math> are in <math>S_{n+1}</math>
# the set <math>\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in M^n : x_1=x_n\}</math> is in <math>S_n</math>
# if <math>D\in S_{n+1}</math> and <math>\pi:M^{n+1}\to M^n</math> is the projection map on the first <math>n</math> coordinates, then <math>\pi(D)\in S_n</math>.

For a subset <math>A</math> of <math>M</math>, we consider the smallest structure <math>S(A)</math> containing <math>S</math> such that every finite subset of <math>A</math> is contained in <math>S_1</math>. A subset <math>D</math> of <math>M^n</math> is called <math>A</math>-definable if it is contained in <math>S_n(A)</math>; in that case, <math>A</math> is called a set of parameters for <math>D</math>. A subset is called definable if it is <math>A</math>-definable for some <math>A</math>.

If <math>M</math> has a dense linear order without endpoints on it, say <math> < </math>, then a structure <math>S</math> on <math>M</math> is called o-minimal (with respect to <math> < </math>) if it satisfies the extra axioms

<ol start="6">
<li>the set <math><</math> (identified with its graph <math>\{(x, y) \in M^2: x < y\}</math>) is in <math>S_2</math>
<li>the definable subsets of <math>M</math> are precisely the finite unions of intervals and points.
</ol>

The "o" stands for "order", since any o-minimal structure requires an ordering on the underlying set.

==Model theoretic definition==

O-minimal structures originated in model theory and so have a simpler—but equivalent—definition using the language of model theory.<ref>Marker (2002) p.81</ref>  Namely, if <math>L</math> is a language including a binary relation <math> < </math>, and <math>(M,<,\dots)</math> is an <math>L</math>-structure where <math> < </math> is interpreted to satisfy the axioms of a dense linear order,<ref>The condition that the interpretation of < be dense is not strictly necessary, but it is known that discrete orders lead to essentially trivial o-minimal structures, see, for example, {{MR|0899083}} and {{MR|0943306}}.</ref> then <math>(M,<,\dots)</math> is called an o-minimal structure if for any definable set <math>X\subseteq M</math> there are finitely many open intervals <math>I_1,\dots,I_r</math> in <math>M\cup \{\pm\infty\}</math> and a finite set <math>X_0</math> such that
:<math>X=X_0\cup I_1\cup\ldots\cup I_r.</math>

==Examples==

Examples of o-minimal theories are:
* The complete theory of dense linear orders in the language with just the ordering.
* RCF, the [[theory]] of [[real closed field]]s.<ref>Marker (2002) p.99</ref>
* The complete theory of the [[real number|real field]] with restricted [[analytic function]]s added (i.e., analytic functions on a neighborhood of <math>[0,1]^n</math>, restricted to <math>[0,1]^n</math>; note that the unrestricted sine function has infinitely many roots, and so cannot be definable in an o-minimal structure.)
* The complete theory of the real field with a symbol for the [[exponential function]] by [[Wilkie's theorem]]. More generally, the complete theory of the real numbers with [[Pfaffian function]]s added.
* The last two examples can be combined: given any o-minimal expansion of the real field (such as the real field with restricted analytic functions), one can define its Pfaffian closure, which is again an o-minimal structure.<ref>Patrick Speisseger, ''Pfaffian sets and o-minimality,'' in: Lecture notes on o-minimal structures and real analytic geometry, C. Miller, J.-P. Rolin, and P. Speissegger (eds.), Fields Institute Communications vol. 62, 2012, pp.&nbsp;179–218. {{doi|10.1007/978-1-4614-4042-0_5}}</ref> (The Pfaffian closure of a structure is, in particular, closed under Pfaffian chains where arbitrary definable functions are used in place of polynomials.)

In the case of RCF, the definable sets are the [[semialgebraic set]]s. Thus the study of o-minimal structures and theories generalises [[real algebraic geometry]]. A major line of current research is based on discovering expansions of the real ordered field that are o-minimal. Despite the generality of application, one can show a great deal about the geometry of set definable in o-minimal structures. There is a cell decomposition theorem,<ref>Marker (2002) p.103</ref> [[Hassler Whitney|Whitney]] and [[Jean-Louis Verdier|Verdier]] [[Stratification (mathematics)|stratification]] theorems and a good notion of dimension and Euler characteristic.

Moreover, continuously differentiable definable functions in a o-minimal structure satisfy a generalization of [[Łojasiewicz inequality]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kurdyka |first=Krzysztof |date=1998 |title=On gradients of functions definable in o-minimal structures |url=https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/item/AIF_1998__48_3_769_0/ |journal=Annales de l'Institut Fourier |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=769–783 |doi=10.5802/aif.1638 |issn=0373-0956|doi-access=free }}</ref> a property that has been used to guarantee the convergence of some non-smooth optimization methods, such as the stochastic subgradient method (under some mild assumptions).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Damek |last2=Drusvyatskiy |first2=Dmitriy |last3=Kakade |first3=Sham |last4=Lee |first4=Jason D. |date=2020 |title=Stochastic Subgradient Method Converges on Tame Functions |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s10208-018-09409-5 |journal=Foundations of Computational Mathematics |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=119–154 |doi=10.1007/s10208-018-09409-5 |arxiv=1804.07795 |s2cid=5025719 |issn=1615-3375}}</ref><ref>{{Cite thesis |title=Descent dynamical systems and algorithms for tame optimization, and multi-objective problems |url=https://tel.archives-ouvertes.fr/tel-02023313 |publisher=Université Montpellier; Universidad técnica Federico Santa María (Valparaiso, Chili) |date=2015-11-02 |degree=PhD |language=en |first=Guillaume |last=Garrigos}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ioffe |first=A. D. |date=2009 |title=An Invitation to Tame Optimization |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/080722059 |journal=SIAM Journal on Optimization |language=en |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=1894–1917 |doi=10.1137/080722059 |issn=1052-6234|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
